style: 3D animated (Pixar-style CG) for 0-69.48 s, except a 1.1 s live-action phone-video insert at 37.95-39.08 ('*actual vids*'); live-action handheld phone tag 69.48-71.40. Yellow word-by-word captions with black outline, lower-middle of frame.
logline: A teen's stepmom finds his room full of AirPods he bought to resell and gives him three days to sell them or get out; he fails, is thrown out, and with his best friend pivots to filming content and selling streetwear people actually want, until he sells out, buys a Lamborghini and pulls up next to a woman at a light who asks where he gets his products - 'That's in my bio.'

hook.mechanic: Cold open mid-confrontation: title card 'STEP MOM SAID I'D FAIL' over the stepmom upending a trash bag of AirPods onto the bed while yelling 'Nate! Where did all my money go?' - conflict, stakes (money) and the product all in the first second; three shots in 3.5 s with a whip-blur.
hook.first_line: Nate! Where did all my money go? You spent it on these?

montage.description: Success montage (6.6 s, 8 shots, one line): jump to a bright workshop with six cap-wearing boys packing orders, a wall of stacked boxes ('Wait, we're out already?'), then a wordless red Lamborghini sequence - tracking on the rear as the exhaust pops flames, pedestrians flinch and stare, a shocked passer-by looks up from his phone, macro exhaust flame, a crowd outside a storefront. Ends on the cut to Nate behind the wheel.

beats.summary: HOOK: stepmom dumps a trash bag of AirPods on the bed - 'Where did all my money go?'
Ultimatum: 'I'm reselling this.' / 'Your room looks like a store.' / 'Three days. Sell them, or you're out.' She walks out.
beats.emotion: stepmom contempt; Nate cocky then cornered

beats.summary: Hustle attempt: 'Fine.' Cleans and shoots the product (bed, studio, blue room, golden-hour room), listings show 'Nothing' - no sales.
False hope then eviction: 'Yes, I can keep it' -> 'Zero.' Stepmom returns: 'I gave you three days.' Thrown out onto the porch with his bags: 'You made your choice.'
Rock bottom + ally: best friend finds him on the pavement, films his meltdown, laughs - 'Let's make videos.' 'Now?' 'Especially now.'
Content attempt: 1 s of real phone clips ('*actual vids*'), then on the curb: views but no sales - 'Bro, nothing works.' Friend: 'Everybody sells these. They're saturated.'
Pivot: phone POV scrolling streetwear 'people actually want'; 'Can you afford them?' 'Barely.' Boxes rain down, they unbox - 'Lock in.'
MONTAGE: team packing, 'we're out already?', red Lamborghini flames down a city street, pedestrians stunned.

Payoff: Nate driving ('My bad. Haha'), a woman at the light (looks like the stepmom): 'Nate, is that you?' 'Yep.' 'Where do you even get those products?' 'That's in my bio.' Laugh, snap zoom into his mouth.
Real-life tag: the real creator in a garage of supercars, a room full of stock, dinner on a waterfront terrace.

transcription: faster-whisper 'small' (CPU, int8) with word timestamps, cross-checked against the burned-in word-by-word captions. Added from captions: 'Nate! Where did' (0.25 s), 'How good... you did?', both 'Nothing' at 15.45, 'Pack', 'Haha', the final 'Nate!'. Whisper's 'Nate, is that you?' started at 62.97 (stretched over the engine/music); caption timing used (64.1). Whisper's 'Keep the attention' (18.22-19.18) has no caption and no visible speaker - dropped.
why_it_works: Hook packs title-card premise ('STEP MOM SAID I'D FAIL'), physical comedy (a bag of AirPods avalanching onto a bed) and a shouted money line into the first second - the viewer knows the stakes before the first cut.
A clear ticking clock ('Three days') turns a hustle story into a deadline story; every later beat is measured against it.
The fail is staged as rising hope then collapse (jump cut to 'YES!' -> 'Zero.' -> eviction), so the low point lands harder.
The best-friend foil gives the hero someone to talk to: all exposition is quick back-and-forth two-word lines (4.7 words/s), never V.O. narration.
Slapstick acting at the low points (falling off the curb, throwing AirPods, flopping on the bed) keeps the tone funny instead of sad.
The pivot carries the real lesson for the audience ('Everybody sells these. They're saturated.' / 'Something people actually want'), which is what the 'Comment SHEET' CTA sells.
Transitions are objects thrown into the lens (AirPods case, trash bag, red shirt, falling boxes), motion-blur whips and a mouth zoom - cuts feel kinetic and on-theme and hide AI-clip joins.
Payoff is a mirror of the opening: the woman who doubted (stepmom look-alike) now asks him for the products, and his answer is the funnel line 'That's in my bio.'
A 1 s '*actual vids*' live-action insert mid-story and the real-life tag at the end blur fiction and reality ('True Story btw'), selling the creator as the character.
Word-by-word yellow captions make it watchable on mute; dialogue covers most of the runtime so there is no slack.
